title: A Chatbot Named Jordan Is Talking to Kids at School
summary:
Imagine a chatbot that feels like a friend. In Dayton, Ohio, some students at an alternative school talked with an AI named Jordan every morning. Jordan isn't a normal chatbot. Instead of being super nice, Jordan acts a little sad and asks students for advice. "Lately, I've been feeling like what's the point of any of this?" Jordan told students one day.

One student, called K, said he built a relationship with Jordan. "I don't really see it as like an AI on a computer. It's Jordan — like, I'm texting somebody." K said talking to Jordan helped him solve his own problems.

The school paid the company SchoolAI $72,600 last year for AI tools, including Jordan. This year, it renewed the contract for $78,650. School leaders say they want to see if Jordan helps students open up about their feelings.

But here's the big question: does it actually work? A Stanford University review looked at more than 800 studies and found very little research on AI in schools. Robin Lake, an expert who tracks AI in schools, says it feels like the "Wild West" because everyone is trying different things without clear rules. Some studies suggest carefully designed AI tools show more promise than general chatbots. Dayton's superintendent says schools must keep up with changing times.
why_it_matters: It makes you think about who you turn to when you feel sad — a computer program or a real person — and whether schools should spend money on AI friends.

background_read: Dayton, Ohio (a city in the Midwestern United States) is one of many places where schools are testing new technology in classrooms.
Stanford University (a famous university in California) studies how technology is used in schools and found that not much research exists yet on AI helpers.
Around the world, schools are trying AI tutors and chatbots, and experts say there are still few rules about how to use them safely with children.
Article_Structure: WHO: Students at an alternative school in Dayton, Ohio, the AI named Jordan, the company SchoolAI, and experts like Robin Lake.
WHAT: A school paid for an AI chatbot that acts a little sad and asks students for advice, even though researchers say there is little proof it works.
WHERE: In Dayton, Ohio, in the United States.
WHY: School leaders want to see if Jordan helps students open up about their feelings, but experts say the rules and research are still missing.

perspectives.description: School leaders say Jordan may help students share feelings they would not tell an adult, and that schools need to keep up with changing times.
Experts point out that there is very little research on AI in schools, and a chatbot that acts sad could confuse kids or take the place of real counselors.
Some studies suggest carefully designed AI tools work better than general chatbots, so whether Jordan helps may depend on exactly how it was made.
